jorden Peterson often calls the Bible the "biblical library" on stage when giving lectures 

this got me thinking about words (again). this is something I can use as an example to illustrate this simple word trick (which acts as a constructor that has measurable phenomnonological effects)

calling the Bible a "biblical library" does 2 things. firstly, it expands the ontological detail. you might not know the Bible is not one book with chapters and that it is rather a collection of books. this detail helps explain things like the inconsistency in style or content across chapters (which you might have implicitly wondered about, as a vague proxy question of "why does this text have an unfamiliar type of complexity"). this is something almost everyone already knows at this point, so I'd posit the main purpose of this word choice is something else.

that brings us to the second thing it does. it changes the axiological weighting, calling it the Bible or a book is a very compressed concept, it streamlines the understanding, throwing away a lot of depth in favor of efficiency. calling it the "biblical library" breaks out of the mold and adds more depth back to it, it's an unfamiliar and more particular way of framing a familiar concept, it adds a richness to the connotation landscape or semantic network, which might inadvertently increase the value placed on the book in your mind through framing

these axiological movements are just as important in rhetoric and communication as ontological extrapolation

it would in fact be impossible to understand what is being said if we only account for ontology and not axiology (which is the exact problem with legalese and classical text)

how information is weighted in value space is how it gets packed into the mind of the audience

how information should be packed (the aesthetic) is as an objective question as any ontological question, even if our methods to answer this are more rudimentary (consisting almost entirely of feeling)

@O_oNevermore the mark of a rationalist vs post rationalist is believing in "aesthetics contain information"

In other words, as @Ματταθίας said to me in person the other day, "ad hominem is not a logical fallacy. The fact that you react differently based on who said it, or _how_ someone said it, is because you are reacting to different information, not noise"

The additional question I'd like to propose here is: when does the intuitive mind update?

(like, the rational mind updates on new, logical information or deduction. But the heart / intuition does not update that way. What _does_ trigger it to update? Can you articulate precisely that mechanism?)

I think the correct answer here, and this is how I would test if someone is at a minimum level of understanding to contribute to discussions of "aesthetics-as-information", is that the update to intuition happens only when an update to reality happens

it features a lot of topics but importantly I think truth should be split up into:
 
- observation/frame ( I keep seeing this person starve with the food they get for lunch)

- Perceived problem (kids dont get enough lunch food/ no child should starve etc)

- cause (capitalism/prinicpals waste too much money, they arent aware, etc)

- solution (hire more etc)

- effect ( kids go to school less)

Which, the effect, can loop back into a new observation.

In particular, truth is only as good as its frame and what it evaluates. In general, I think the ability to evaluate truth frames is pretty lacking culturally and it's more than people are bad at epistemology. Plenty of frames can be evaluated as true but are useless.
